cues.text: Three Days of Exposition

In 1608, the Benedictine monks of the abbey at Faverney, in the Franche-Comte region of France, had papal permission to expose the Blessed Sacrament for three days of public veneration around the feast of Pentecost.
On the eve of the feast, May 24, they set two Hosts in a large monstrance on a provisional altar of repose and left two oil lamps burning before it overnight.
A Church Full of Smoke
Early the next morning, the sacristan, Dom Garnier, opened the church doors and found them filled with smoke.
The provisional altar was already engulfed in flames that would reduce it entirely to ashes, melting even a nearby metal chandelier with the heat.
He raised the alarm, and the monks rushed to fight the blaze alongside him.
Suspended Above the Ruins
As the fire was finally brought under control and the smoke began to clear, a young novice named Hudelot noticed something.
The older monks had missed it in the chaos: the monstrance itself, holding both Hosts, was hovering in midair above the wreckage of the altar.
It was unsupported by anything beneath it, leaning gently toward the grille at the back where the altar had stood.
A Vigil of Thirty-Three Hours
Unsure how to respond, the monks summoned Capuchin friars from nearby Vesoul.
They built a new altar directly beneath the suspended monstrance and celebrated Mass.
At the moment of elevation, the monstrance descended slowly on its own to rest on the new altar.
It had remained aloft for some thirty-three hours in all.
Both Hosts, examined afterward, were found completely unharmed by the fire that had destroyed everything around them.
Legacy
The Archbishop of Besancon declared the event authentic on July 10, 1608, and Pope Paul V granted a bull of indulgence later that same year after the miracle was reported to Rome.
One of the two Hosts was later transferred to Dole for safekeeping and was destroyed in the French Revolution.
The second survives and remains venerated at Faverney today, carried each year in the same monstrance.
That monstrance — rebuilt after the original's own destruction in the Revolution — first held it suspended above a burning altar four centuries ago.
